1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# scripts/lib/stage-limits.sh — the limits a stage's model calls run under.
3	#
4	# One copy, two readers: the router enforces these numbers on every call
5	# (core/router/route.sh) and the engine states them to the stage in its rules
6	# (scripts/lib/stage-prompt.sh, ADR-067 §8). A stage told a different budget
7	# from the one it is killed at works until it is killed.
8	#
9	# Sourced library: inherits the caller's shell options; do NOT add set -euo.
10	[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_STAGE_LIMITS_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
11	_ZBUILD_STAGE_LIMITS_LOADED=1
12	
13	if ! declare -F manifest_router_knob >/dev/null 2>&1; then
14	    # shellcheck source=../../core/plugin-registry/manifest-router-budget.sh
15	    source "$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}" 2>/dev/null || true; cd "../.." && pwd)/core/plugin-registry/manifest-router-budget.sh" 2>/dev/null || true
16	fi
17	
18	# ─── _route_manifest_knob <knob> — ADR-017 §11 (#1816) manifest layer ───────
19	# The dispatched plugin's OWN declared default, read from its manifest via the
20	# dispatch identity the engine exports at plugin_hook_call (ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR,
21	# ADR-054 §3 / #1862). Empty whenever there is no dispatch, no manifest, no
22	# declaration — or a declaration this router cannot use.
23	#
24	# Out-of-range and non-numeric values are IGNORED here, not fatal: the loud
25	# gate is validate_manifest at load, and a plugin that got past it with a bad
26	# value must fall back to the constant rather than hand the router a 0-second
27	# timeout. Fail-safe on the hot path, fail-loud at the boundary.
28	_route_manifest_knob() {
29	    local knob="$1"
30	    local dir="${ZBUILD_PLUGIN_DIR:-}"
31	    [[ -n "$dir" && -f "$dir/manifest.yaml" ]] || return 0
32	    declare -F manifest_router_knob >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 0
33	    local v; v="$(manifest_router_knob "$dir/manifest.yaml" "$knob" 2>/dev/null || true)"
34	    [[ "$v" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
35	    local range; range="$(_manifest_router_range "$knob" 2>/dev/null || true)"
36	    [[ -n "$range" ]] || return 0
37	    local min="${range% *}" max="${range#* }"
38	    [[ "$v" -ge "$min" && "$v" -le "$max" ]] || return 0
39	    printf '%s' "$v"
40	}
41	
42	# ─── _route_resolve_knob — ADR-017 (#455) precedence chokepoint ──────────────
43	# Generic helper: future knobs (tier_default, budget_usd, model_override) reuse
44	# this. Accessor returns per-stage value or empty; env_var supplies session-wide
45	# fallback; manifest_knob (#1816) names the plugin's own declared default; the
46	# compile-time constant is the floor:
47	#
48	#   template accessor  >  env var  >  manifest config.router.*  >  constant
49	#
50	# The manifest sits BELOW env and template because it is a default, not an
51	# override: a flow may right-size a stage for a fast lane, and the operator
52	# escape hatch must still beat both. It sits ABOVE the constant because that is
53	# what the constant always was — a default nobody could state per stage.
54	_route_resolve_knob() {
55	    local accessor_fn="$1" env_var="$2" default_val="$3"
56	    local override_event="${4:-router.timeout.override_ignored}"
57	    local manifest_knob="${5:-}"
58	    local v=""
59	    if [[ -n "${ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE:-}" ]] && declare -F "$accessor_fn" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
60	        v="$($accessor_fn "$ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE" 2>/dev/null || true)"
61	    fi
62	    if [[ -n "$v" ]]; then
63	        # If env var ALSO set and differs, emit override-ignored event for audit.
64	        # A manifest value losing to template or env is NOT this case: a default
65	        # being replaced is the design, and eventing it would make every
66	        # declaring plugin noisy on every dispatch.
67	        local env_val="${!env_var:-}"
68	        if [[ -n "$env_val" && "$env_val" != "$v" ]]; then
69	            eb_emit_event "$override_event" \
70	                "stage=${ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE:-}" \
71	                "env_var=$env_var" \
72	                "env_value=$env_val" \
73	                "applied=$v" 2>/dev/null || true
74	        fi
75	        printf '%s\n' "$v"; return 0
76	    fi
77	    local env_v="${!env_var:-}"
78	    if [[ -n "$env_v" ]]; then
79	        printf '%s\n' "$env_v"; return 0
80	    fi
81	    if [[ -n "$manifest_knob" ]]; then
82	        local mv; mv="$(_route_manifest_knob "$manifest_knob")"
83	        if [[ -n "$mv" ]]; then
84	            printf '%s\n' "$mv"; return 0
85	        fi
86	    fi
87	    printf '%s\n' "$default_val"
88	}
89	
90	# Concrete: per-stage router.timeout_s > $ZBUILD_ROUTER_TIMEOUT >
91	# manifest config.router.timeout_s > 300s default.
92	_route_resolve_timeout() {
93	    _route_resolve_knob template_stage_router_timeout ZBUILD_ROUTER_TIMEOUT 300 \
94	        router.timeout.override_ignored timeout_s
95	}
96	
97	# ADR-018 (#466): per-stage router.max_turns > $ZBUILD_ROUTER_MAX_TURNS > 25 default.
98	# ADR-029 G3 (#812): when the cycle orchestrator detects a router timeout for
99	# this stage, it sets ZBUILD_ROUTER_MAX_TURNS_OVERRIDE so the next dispatch

101	# override wins over the per-stage template AND the env knob because that's
102	# the entire point — escalation must beat the static config that already
103	# proved too small.

105	    if [[ "${ZBUILD_ROUTER_MAX_TURNS_OVERRIDE:-}" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then

108	    fi

129	    elif [[ "${ZBUILD_ROUTER_MAX_TURNS:-}" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] && [[ "${ZBUILD_ROUTER_MAX_TURNS}" -eq 0 ]]; then

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# tests/unit/run-watchdog-clean-exit-test.sh — clean-exit watchdog lifecycle (#1944)
3	#
4	# SPEC-3 [code]:
5	#   A run that finishes within max_run_s exits with its own pipeline status
6	#   unchanged; the watchdog process does not exist after the runner process exits.
7	#
8	# A test that only checks "runner exits 0" passes BEFORE implementation too.

10	#   1. _runner_resolve_run_limit_s is defined (fails before implementation)
11	#   2. With ZBUILD_MAX_RUN_S set, the completed run's status is the stage-reported
12	#      status — not timed_out (impl must not fire the watchdog on a clean run)
13	#   3. No pipeline.end status=timed_out in the events log (watchdog was reaped)
14	#   4. Watchdog process is dead after runner exits: abort sentinel is NOT written
15	#      after the runner exits — an un-reaped watchdog would write it when it fires.

18	SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"

34	# shellcheck source=../../scripts/lib/stage-limits.sh
35	source "$STAGE_LIMITS" 2>/dev/null || true
36	
37	if declare -F _runner_resolve_run_limit_s >/dev/null 2>&1; then
38	    assert_pass "[#1944/SPEC-3] _runner_resolve_run_limit_s is defined"
39	else
40	    assert_fail "[#1944/SPEC-3] _runner_resolve_run_limit_s is defined" \
41	        "function not found; watchdog arms only when this function exists"
42	fi

content.text:
I now have a complete picture. Here are all findings:

---

**FINDING 1 — Race condition: watchdog writes sentinel then sends SIGTERM; EXIT trap can clear sentinel before SIGTERM fires**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, lines 2849-2850 (watchdog body) and line 2608 (abort trap).

The watchdog does:
```
_zbuild_arm_abort_sentinel timed_out    # writes to _ZB_ABORT_REASON + file
kill -TERM -- "-${_wdg_pgid}"          # sends signal to process group
```
Between these two lines, if the runner's stage dispatch returns 0 and the stage loop runs to completion (hitting `_runner_ended=true` and then `exit 0`), the EXIT trap fires first, calls `_zbuild_disarm_abort_sentinel` (line 2608), and clears both `_ZB_ABORT_REASON` and the sentinel file. When SIGTERM eventually lands, `_runner_signal_trap` calls `_zbuild_arm_abort_sentinel "sigterm"`, which re-arms with "sigterm" (since the prior `timed_out` was just erased). `_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON` is then set to "sigterm", not "timed_out". The run ends as "interrupted" instead of "timed_out".

Severity: real race in practice only in a narrow window (the stage completes in the microseconds between sentinel-write and SIGTERM delivery), but the signal delivery path is correct. The main mitigation is that the sentinel write happens before `kill`, so on most architectures SIGTERM lands before the process group can do significant work. However, this is a genuine TOCTOU: there is no atomic "write-then-signal" primitive here. The comment at line 2825 acknowledges "first-wins preserves `timed_out`" but the disarm happens before the signal is confirmed delivered.

**FINDING 2 — Race condition: SIGTERM re-arm window between watchdog `wait` and trap reinstall**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, lines 2570-2579.

The abort trap installs `trap ':' INT TERM` at line 2551 (via `_runner_restore_stderr` at line 2939, and the explicit reinstall at 2551). After killing the watchdog (`kill -KILL` at line 2570) and waiting for it (line 2571), it kills orphaned children (lines 2573-2578), and then at line 2579 reinstalls:
```
trap '_runner_signal_trap TERM' TERM
trap '_runner_signal_trap INT' INT
```
The kill-orphans loop (lines 2573-2578) runs with `trap ':' TERM` in effect, but between line 2578 and line 2579, bash checks pending signals at statement boundaries. This is the period between `_runner_dispatch_always_run` dispatch and the `trap` reinstall at line 2579 — wait, the reinstall is at 2579, before `_runner_dispatch_always_run`. The window where `trap ':' TERM` is active and a second SIGTERM would be silently eaten includes the entire always-run dispatch block (lines 2583-2633). This is the intended behavior per the comment at lines 2548-2550, but it means an operator kill during always-run teardown is silently eaten. That may be a documented trade-off, not a bug.

**FINDING 3 — Logic error: `_at_abort_word` captured from `_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON` which is NOT set when timed_out arrives via pre-flight check (not signal path)**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, lines 2601 and 3833-3836.

The linear dispatch loop's pre-flight check (line 3833) runs `_zbuild_check_abort`, and if the abort is `timed_out`, it does:
```bash
_RUNNER_SIGINT_RECEIVED=1
_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON="$(_zbuild_abort_reason)"   # correctly set to "timed_out"
return 1
```
This `return 1` propagates upward until `set -e` triggers the EXIT trap. At the abort trap, `_at_abort_word="${_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON:-}"` reads "timed_out" correctly.

However, the cycle dispatch path at line 3834-3835 also sets `_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON` correctly. This is fine.

The actual risk is different: the `_runner_end_on_abort` function at line 2991 calls `_zbuild_abort_reason` *directly* (not `_RUNNER_ABORT_REASON`), so it reads from `_ZB_ABORT_REASON` or the sentinel file. When `_runner_end_on_abort` handles `timed_out`, it sets `_runner_ended=true` (line 3015) and returns 1. This triggers `set -e`, then the EXIT trap. The EXIT trap's short-circuit at line 2620 fires because `_runner_ended == "true"`, so it calls `_runner_status_comment_reap` and returns without re-emitting `pipeline.end`. That is correct.

But: `_runner_end_on_abort`'s timed_out arm (line 3007-3016) does **not** emit `pipeline.aborted` — only `pipeline.end`. The other arms (llm_unavailable, interrupted) emit both `pipeline.aborted` and `pipeline.end`. This is a protocol asymmetry: consumers that listen for `pipeline.aborted` to detect a timeout will never receive one. This is a design flaw, not a crash, but it affects observability.

**FINDING 4 — TOCTOU: `_wdg_orphans` collected before watchdog is killed, but watchdog has 10 seconds to spawn MORE children**

**FINDING 8 — Empty `_RUNNER_WATCHDOG_PID` kill is safe but for wrong reason**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, line 2570.

```bash
kill -KILL "${_RUNNER_WATCHDOG_PID:-}" 2>/dev/null || true
```

If `_RUNNER_WATCHDOG_PID` is empty, this expands to `kill -KILL ""`. On Linux bash, `kill -KILL ""` with an empty string fails with "invalid signal specification" or similar, which is suppressed by `2>/dev/null || true`. On some implementations, `kill ""` kills process 0 or the current process group — this would be a self-kill. Testing: in bash, `kill -KILL ""` produces "kill: : invalid signal specification" and returns non-zero; it does NOT send a signal to the process group. So the `|| true` makes this safe. However, the original concern is valid: on older bash or different implementations this behavior is not specified. A guard `[[ -n "${_RUNNER_WATCHDOG_PID:-}" ]] && kill -KILL "$_RUNNER_WATCHDOG_PID" ...` would be safer, and it is applied for the `wait` on line 2571 but not for the `kill` on line 2570. **FINDING 9 — P3 test: `trap '' TERM` in plugin function body does NOT run in the runner's shell**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/tests/integration/run-timed-out-test.sh`, lines 300-310.

The plugin function `slow_stage_run` runs inside a subshell spawned by `plugin_hook_call`. The `trap '' TERM` inside that function sets TERM to be ignored in that subshell's process, not in the runner's shell. The runner's TERM trap (`_runner_signal_trap TERM`) remains installed in the runner process. When the watchdog sends `kill -TERM -- "-${_wdg_pgid}"` to the process group, the runner receives SIGTERM (fires `_runner_signal_trap`) and the plugin subshell has `trap '' TERM` so it ignores it. The escalation `kill -KILL "$_wdg_child"` (10s later) targets runner children via `pgrep -P "$_wdg_runner_pid"`. The plugin subshell is a child of the runner process, so it will be found and killed. This is working as designed. The test is correct.

However, there is a subtle issue: `trap '' TERM` is set inside a bash function, not at the subshell level. In bash, `trap` inside a function changes the trap for the current shell, not a forked subshell. The plugin function is called inside `plugin_hook_call` which runs as `( ... ) &` — that subshell inherits the runner's TERM trap and the function body's `trap '' TERM` then modifies it. This is intentional. The test correctly exercises the KILL escalation path. Not a bug.

**FINDING 10 — P2 timing bounds are fragile on loaded CI infrastructure**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/tests/integration/run-timed-out-test.sh`, lines 279-291.

- Global watchdog (correct): fires at t=6s from start; SIGKILL at ~16s; cleanup by ~18s.
- Per-stage reset (wrong): fires at ~11s; SIGKILL at ~21s; cleanup at ~23s.

- If `fast-one`'s `sleep 5` takes 6s on a loaded machine, the global watchdog fires during fast-one (violating the "fast-one completed" check).
- If overhead after SIGKILL is > 2s, the elapsed-time assertion fails even on a correct global watchdog implementation.

The 20s bound provides only a 2s margin above the expected 18s path, and the "fast-one completed" check assumes `fast-one` finishes in <6s, which has the same 1-second margin. This test would be expected to flake on a CI runner under >1s scheduling jitter. This is a missing-deliverable concern: the issue acceptance criteria says the test must "reden at the merge-base" robustly, but the timing margins are too tight for reliable CI behavior.

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, lines 2790-2865.

This is arguably correct behavior. Not a flaw.

**FINDING 12 — S3-4 test: the sentinel check is insufficient to verify watchdog was reaped**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/tests/unit/run-watchdog-clean-exit-test.sh`, lines 115-171.

The test checks that after `sleep 5` (past max_run_s=4), the sentinel file is absent and the pipeline-state.json does not show `timed_out`. However, if the watchdog is orphaned and its `sleep 4` child fires, the watchdog calls `_zbuild_arm_abort_sentinel timed_out` — which writes to the sentinel AND calls `kill -TERM -- "-${_wdg_pgid}"`. That SIGTERM hits the runner's process group. But the runner has already exited, so the process group no longer exists. The only process that could receive it is the test shell itself (if it is still in that group). The test shell does not have a TERM trap installed, so it would die, causing the test to exit non-zero (different from a clean assertion failure).

More critically: the test waits 5s after the runner exits (line 144), which is past max_run_s=4. An un-reaped watchdog would have fired at max_run_s=4 seconds after the runner started (not after it exited). The runner exits quickly (< 2s), so max_run_s=4 elapses during the sleep 5. But the sentinel write only happens inside the watchdog's subshell process. After the runner exits, the watchdog subshell (if not reaped) is reparented to init. The `_zbuild_arm_abort_sentinel` function requires `ZBUILD_STATE_DIR` to be set. In the watchdog subshell, `ZBUILD_STATE_DIR` was inherited from the runner process at fork time, so it is still set. The sentinel file path is valid. So yes, an un-reaped watchdog can and will write the sentinel. The test correctly detects this.

However, the state-file check (`_post_sleep_status`) at lines 152-160 is the primary gate. An un-reaped watchdog would: (1) write the sentinel, (2) send SIGTERM to the dead process group (no-op), and (3) wait 10s, then try to `pgrep -P` the dead runner PID (no children; loop does nothing). Only the SIGTERM-to-runner path (inside the runner) calls `_set_pipeline_status`. Therefore the pipeline-state.json check in S3-4 is testing the wrong thing: it would pass even if the watchdog fires (because the watchdog itself never writes to pipeline-state.json). The sentinel-absence check at line 165 is the correct discriminator.

Severity: test logic flaw. The `_post_sleep_status` assertion at line 152 is presented as a primary check but cannot actually detect an orphaned watchdog because the watchdog doesn't touch pipeline-state.json. The test would pass falsely if the sentinel were not checked. The sentinel check at line 165 saves it, but the test comment and structure imply the state file check is the key assertion.

**FINDING 13 — `_runner_end_on_abort` timed_out arm: `pipeline.aborted` event is never emitted**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, lines 3007-3016.

The `timed_out` case emits `pipeline.end status=timed_out` but never emits `pipeline.aborted`. The `llm_unavailable` and interrupt arms each emit `pipeline.aborted` before `pipeline.end`. Consumers subscribing to `pipeline.aborted` to detect run termination will miss the timed_out case. The abort trap's timed_out arm (lines 2621-2633) also only emits `pipeline.end` with no `pipeline.aborted`. This is internally consistent (both paths agree), but it diverges from the protocol of every other non-clean exit path. Any consumer that uses `pipeline.aborted` to trigger postmortem analysis would silently miss timed-out runs. This is a protocol flaw that could allow a monitoring or alerting system to classify a timed-out run as successful or to miss it entirely.

**FINDING 14 — Watchdog KILL escalation targets runner's children via `pgrep -P runner_pid`, not the stage's PGID**

File: `/home/runner/.zbuild/repos/ezigus/zBuild/issues/1944/worktree/core/pipeline/runner.sh`, lines 2854-2863.

The escalation block enumerates `pgrep -P "$_wdg_runner_pid"` (direct children of the runner). However, a stage that spawns its own subprocess tree (grandchildren of the runner) will not be found by this single-level `pgrep -P` call. Only direct children of the runner process are killed. If the stage function spawned a background job that in turn spawned additional processes, those grandchildren survive the KILL escalation indefinitely. The SIGTERM at line 2850 to the process group should have reached them, but if they too have `trap '' TERM` or `SIG_IGN` inherited, they will outlive the watchdog's escalation. There is no recursive kill here.

This is not a security escalation in the classic sense, but it is a resource leak that defeats the stated purpose of the escalation block ("a process that ignores TERM is dead within TERM + 10 s"). A deeply nested subprocess tree with `trap '' TERM` at multiple levels would survive indefinitely after the runner exits.

---

**Summary of highest-severity findings:**

1. **FINDING 1** — Real race: sentinel cleared by EXIT trap before SIGTERM delivered; timed_out reverts to interrupted. Exploitable in tight timing.
2. **FINDING 13** — Protocol flaw: `pipeline.aborted` never emitted for timed_out; monitoring consumers silently miss timeout events.
3. **FINDING 12** — Test flaw: S3-4 primary assertion (state-file check) cannot detect orphaned watchdog; only the sentinel check is correct.
4. **FINDING 10** — Flakiness risk: P2 timing margins (2s headroom on 20s bound) will produce false failures on loaded CI systems.
5. **FINDING 14** — Incomplete kill escalation: grandchildren with SIG_IGN survive beyond the 10s KILL window.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/lib/abort-propagation.sh — ADR-025 abort-propagation contract (Wave 15-B, #684)
#
# An abort is RECORDED once, as a word, and every dispatcher asks for it at the
# same two points in its loop (#1850, ADR-054 §4 — no rc carries the reason):
#
#   loop {
#       _zbuild_check_abort || return 1             # pre-flight
#       dispatch_child
#       _zbuild_propagate_abort $? || return 1      # post-flight
#   }
#
# Words: sigint | sigterm | cycle_abort | llm_unavailable | llm_rate_limited |
# scope_too_large | timed_out. The first recorded abort wins.
#
# Two channels hold the word: `_ZB_ABORT_REASON` in this process, and the
# sentinel file ${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR}/.abort.signal, which crosses subshells and
# `_zbuild_make_fresh_shell` env scrubs (ADR-024) where a variable does not.
# An EMPTY sentinel reads as `sigint` — what arming wrote before it took a word.
#
# Sourced library: no `set -euo pipefail` (would mutate caller options).

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_ABORT_PROP_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_ABORT_PROP_LOADED=1

# Empty when ZBUILD_STATE_DIR is unset: the helpers then keep the word in-process
# only, rather than fabricate a path under cwd.
_zbuild_abort_sentinel_path() {
    if [[ -n "${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR:-}" ]]; then
        printf '%s/.abort.signal' "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
    fi
}

_zbuild_abort_reason() { local _zar; _zbuild_abort_reason_v _zar; printf '%s' "$_zar"; }
# _zbuild_abort_reason_v <var> — the same into <var>, in this shell: the runner
# checks for an abort after every dispatch.
_zbuild_abort_reason_v() {
    local -n _zaro="$1"
    _zaro=""
    if [[ -n "${_ZB_ABORT_REASON:-}" ]]; then
        _zaro="$_ZB_ABORT_REASON"
        return 0
    fi
    # _zbuild_abort_sentinel_path
    [[ -n "${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR:-}" ]] || return 0
    local _zar_s="$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR/.abort.signal" _zar_w=""
    [[ -e "$_zar_s" ]] || return 0
    IFS= read -r _zar_w 2>/dev/null < "$_zar_s" || true
    _zaro="${_zar_w:-sigint}"
}

# Best-effort: a failed sentinel write must not fail a signal trap — the
# in-process word still holds the abort.
_zbuild_arm_abort_sentinel() {
    local _word="${1:-sigint}" _sentinel _dir _prior
    _prior="$(_zbuild_abort_reason)"
    if [[ -n "$_prior" ]]; then
        _ZB_ABORT_REASON="$_prior"
        return 0
    fi
    _ZB_ABORT_REASON="$_word"
    _sentinel="$(_zbuild_abort_sentinel_path)"
    [[ -z "$_sentinel" ]] && return 0
    _dir="$(dirname "$_sentinel")"
    [[ -d "$_dir" ]] || mkdir -p "$_dir" 2>/dev/null || return 0
    printf '%s\n' "$_word" > "$_sentinel" 2>/dev/null || true
    return 0
}

# Called by the runner's EXIT trap and by --resume, so a later run in the same
# state dir does not see a stale abort.
_zbuild_disarm_abort_sentinel() {
    local _sentinel
    unset _ZB_ABORT_REASON
    _sentinel="$(_zbuild_abort_sentinel_path)"
    [[ -z "$_sentinel" ]] && return 0
    [[ -e "$_sentinel" ]] && rm -f "$_sentinel" 2>/dev/null || true
    return 0
}

# Returns 1 so a caller can write `_zbuild_abort <word>; return` or `|| return 1`.
_zbuild_abort() {
    _zbuild_arm_abort_sentinel "${1:-sigint}"
    return 1
}

_zbuild_check_abort() {
    local _zca; _zbuild_abort_reason_v _zca
    [[ -n "$_zca" ]] && return 1
    return 0
}

# 1 only when the child failed AND an abort is recorded: an ordinary failure is
# the caller's to handle, and a child that succeeded is not an abort.
_zbuild_propagate_abort() {
    [[ "${1:-0}" == "0" ]] && return 0
    _zbuild_check_abort
}

        # Wave 15-H (#688): flag-gated process-group signal forwarding. When
        # `set -m` is on (via ZBUILD_RUNNER_JOB_CONTROL=1 at startup), every
        # child of this shell — backgrounded OR foreground subshell — has its
        # own PGID == its PID, so `kill -- -PID` reaches the whole subtree.
        # We enumerate direct children via two complementary sources:
        #   1. `jobs -p` — backgrounded jobs known to bash
        #   2. `pgrep -P $$` — all direct children, including foreground
        #      subshells bash does NOT list in `jobs -p`
        # We TERM each PGID, then schedule a 1s-grace KILL backstop for any
        # child that traps and ignores TERM. Per-site kills (Wave 8 build
        # plugin, Wave 15-G router) remain as fallback — this is belt-and-
        # suspenders, not replacement.
        #
        # Known limitation: bash defers signal-trap delivery until the
        # current foreground command returns. With `set -m`, a foreground
        # plugin subshell is in its own PGID, so a kernel-pgrp TERM to the
        # runner does NOT reach it directly; the trap fires only after the
        # subshell returns naturally. This is acceptable because:
        #   (a) the flag is OPT-IN (default OFF, byte-identical to today);
        #   (b) the router's Wave 15-G PG-kill already handles the slow
        #       claude-spawning path (the realistic blocker);
        #   (c) plugin dispatch now runs in the background (ADR-054 §7), so
        #       the trap runs at once and plugin_stop_running stops the stage.
        if [[ "${ZBUILD_RUNNER_JOB_CONTROL:-0}" == "1" ]]; then
            local _child_pid _pgid _pgids_snapshot="" _self_pgid=""
            # Resolve the runner's own PGID so we never signal it (would
            # be suicide; the trap's `exit` below handles runner teardown).
            if command -v ps >/dev/null 2>&1; then
                _self_pgid="$(ps -o pgid= -p $$ 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
            fi
            _w15h_collect_pgid() {
                # Resolve a child PID to its current PGID via `ps` (which
                # is reliable even when the PID is not the group leader)
                # and append it to the dedup snapshot. Falls back to the
                # PID itself when `ps` cannot resolve (e.g. child already
                # exited) — kill is best-effort 2>/dev/null anyway.
                local _pid="$1" _resolved=""
                [[ -z "$_pid" ]] && return 0
                # #2131: the status-comment sidecar is reaped by the EXIT
                # trap AFTER pipeline.aborted is on disk — not swept here,
                # where the 1s KILL backstop would cut its final render.
                [[ "$_pid" == "${_RUNNER_STATUS_COMMENT_PID:-}" ]] && return 0
                if command -v ps >/dev/null 2>&1; then
                    _resolved="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$_pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
                fi
                [[ -z "$_resolved" ]] && _resolved="$_pid"
                # Skip runner's own PGID — protects against self-signal
                # when a child's PGID resolved to the runner's group
                # (can happen when `set -m` was not effective for that
                # spawn site, e.g. a sync call that pre-dated the flag).
                [[ -n "$_self_pgid" && "$_resolved" == "$_self_pgid" ]] && return 0
                case " $_pgids_snapshot " in *" $_resolved "*) return 0;; esac
                _pgids_snapshot+="$_resolved "
            }
            # Source 1: bash-tracked background jobs.
            while IFS= read -r _child_pid; do
                _w15h_collect_pgid "$_child_pid"
            done < <(jobs -p 2>/dev/null)
            # Source 2: all direct children (catches foreground subshells
            # which bash does NOT list in `jobs -p`).
            if command -v pgrep >/dev/null 2>&1; then
                while IFS= read -r _child_pid; do
                    _w15h_collect_pgid "$_child_pid"
                done < <(pgrep -P $$ 2>/dev/null)
            fi
            # TERM each unique resolved PGID.
            for _pgid in $_pgids_snapshot; do
                kill -TERM -- "-$_pgid" 2>/dev/null || true
            done
            if [[ -n "$_pgids_snapshot" ]]; then
                ( sleep 1
                  local _pg
                  for _pg in $_pgids_snapshot; do
                      kill -KILL -- "-$_pg" 2>/dev/null || true
                  done
                ) &
                disown $! 2>/dev/null || true
            fi
        fi
        # ADR-054 §11 (#1944): read back the ACTUAL abort reason after arming —
        # if the watchdog wrote `timed_out` before this signal fired, first-wins
        # preserves it; _RUNNER_ABORT_REASON must carry that, not the signal word.
        _RUNNER_ABORT_REASON="$(_zbuild_abort_reason)"
        # Not a clean 0: the parent sees the run failed; why is in the events.
        exit 1
    }
    # The runner's own stderr, for the abort trap (_runner_restore_stderr).
    exec {_RUNNER_ERR_FD}>&2
    trap '_runner_abort_trap' EXIT
